extracted.intended_audience: technology transfer offices, university research administrators, faculty involved in technology/material transfers, and research compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for university technology transfer offices and researchers on when U.S. export controls, ITAR, EAR, and OFAC embargoes apply to transfers of materials, items, technologies, technical data, and written publications, and how to structure agreements and compliance programs to manage those risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult OFAC sanctions lists before transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Before any contract is entered into for the transfer of materials or items or related information, or for the provision of any payment, advice, or service, OFAC sanctions lists should be consulted to ensure that the transfer is not to a prohibited person, entity, or country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the transfer is to a prohibited person/entity/country, the transfer may not be made unless OFAC grants a license. The likelihood of obtaining a license depends on which sanctioned country, individual, or entity is involved, why the sanction was imposed, and the sanction’s terms and conditions. Be aware that OFAC restrictions may still apply even when EAR/ITAR differ; check all relevant lists (e.g., OFAC SDN list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental research exclusion — eligibility conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental research exclusion under EAR and ITAR applies literally to (a) information (but not to export-controlled materials or items) (b) resulting from or arising during 'basic and applied research in science and engineering' (c) conducted at an 'accredited institution of higher education' (EAR) or 'higher learning' (ITAR) (d) 'located in the United States' (e) that is 'ordinarily published and shared broadly within the scientific community' and (f) that is not 'restricted for proprietary reasons or specific national security reasons' (EAR) or subject to 'specific U.S. Government access and dissemination controls' (ITAR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusion permits foreign members of university communities to participate in research involving export-controlled information on campus. It applies to information/technical data only, not to controlled materials or items (except very limited ITAR exceptions). If sponsor or agency conditions require pre-publication approval, restrict access to U.S. citizens, or impose proprietary publication restrictions, the exclusion is destroyed. Short publication delays for sponsor review or to seek patent protection are permitted without destroying the exclusion, but the research results themselves must not be proprietary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental research exclusion — limitations and practical cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions and other conditions limiting access to and dissemination of research results under material transfer and license agreements may arguably destroy the fundamental research and public availability/public domain exclusions from export controls if they are, in effect, proprietary information publication or dissemination restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research licenses that allow unrestricted sublicenses for research use may arguably preserve the exclusions, although expert counsel should be consulted when there is a question. Special care is warranted to determine whether export controls apply to materials or items and related technology/technical data that are subject to exclusive licensing agreements before entering into such agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicly available/public domain exclusion — scope and qualifying methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The public domain exclusion under ITAR and the publicly available exclusion under EAR apply to information (including technologies and technical data) that is already published (not just ordinarily published) through specified means, and consequently is not subject to export controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualifying publication methods include: (a) libraries open to the public; (b) unrestricted subscriptions/newsstands/bookstores sold at a reasonable price; (c) U.S. patents and open (published) patent applications; (d) conferences/meetings/seminars/trade shows/exhibitions held in the U.S. that are generally open to the public for a fee where attendees may take notes and leave with them; and (e) websites accessible to the public, free of charge, without host control of who visits or downloads. These regulatory methods are the only ones that qualify regardless of how widely available the information may be otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public domain/public availability exclusions — limits
rubrics_metrics.description: These exclusions expressly apply only to the export or deemed export of information (including technologies and technical data), not to the export of USML- or CCL-listed or otherwise controlled materials or items, or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify, there must not be a reason to believe that the exported information will be used in or for weapons of mass destruction, and the federal government must not have imposed export controls or restrictions as a funding condition. If an institution or PI agrees to restrict public disclosure or limit foreign-national participation, the information will not qualify for these exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing triggers — ITAR
rubrics_metrics.description: An ITAR license will be required if the proposed export of an ITAR-regulated defense article or related defense service is to an ITAR-prohibited country or a United Nations Security Council arms-embargoed country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exports to ITAR-prohibited or UN arms-embargoed countries are likely to be denied (i.e., prohibited). For other ITAR exports, licenses are considered and granted or denied on a case-by-case basis. The same analysis applies to deemed exports of controlled technical data/technologies in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing triggers — EAR (EAR99, CCL-listed, and special items)
rubrics_metrics.description: An EAR license may be required for proposed exports of materials/items or related technologies/technical data listed on the CCL under the catchall EAR99 category if the export involves an entity/person on the EAR Entity List or Denied Persons List, a prohibited end use (e.g., WMD program), an OFAC-embargoed country, or anyone on OFAC prohibited lists; otherwise EAR99 typically does not require a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For CCL-listed items in categories other than EAR99, license requirements depend on destination, end user, and end use and are assessed case-by-case. Licenses may be required for exports to certain entities/individuals within a country even if exports to others in the same country do not require a license. For many chemicals/biological agents on the CCL, an EAR license is required for export to any country and may be denied for Syria or OFAC-embargoed countries; CWC-listed chemicals may be denied to non-party countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions apply to information, not materials/items
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory exclusions (fundamental research, public domain/publicly available) generally apply to information (technologies and technical data) and do not permit the transfer of controlled materials or items abroad (with very limited ITAR exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when information qualifies for an exclusion, physical materials, equipment, encrypted software, chemicals, biological agents, or services listed on USML/CCL remain subject to export controls; traveling abroad with a computer containing regulated encrypted software may itself be an export.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deemed exports and campus participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deemed exports (disclosure of controlled technical data/technology to foreign nationals in the U.S.) may be allowed under the fundamental research exclusion when research is conducted on campus in the United States in accordance with the exclusion’s prerequisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is ongoing governmental dialogue about whether the exclusion allows deemed exports of controlled technologies that are used in or necessary for, but do not arise from, fundamental research. Academic interpretation has long been that group members must be able to freely disclose among themselves information on how to use controlled equipment; however, this is under government review. Ensure foreign nationals receive otherwise controlled information only on campus where required to preserve the exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsor-imposed publication or foreign-participation restrictions destroy exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a university accepts a condition from a government agency or nongovernment sponsor that requires approval prior to publication of research results, restricts access to research results, or limits participation to U.S. citizens, the fundamental research exclusion is destroyed and export controls apply to controlled materials/items and related information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting such restrictions (rather than using classification where appropriate) conflicts with NSDD 189 principles. Some limited exceptions exist under EAR when the federal government imposes specific national security controls and the university adheres to them; if controls are not satisfied, licensing requirements apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible short delay for publication (sponsor review/patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A short delay in publication only for purposes of allowing sponsor review to ensure that sponsor-provided proprietary information is not inadvertently included or to allow the institution or the sponsor to seek patent protection is permitted without destroying the fundamental research exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The delay must be limited and for those stated purposes; the research results themselves may not be proprietary or the fundamental research exclusion will not apply. Careful coordination between patent filing strategy and eligibility for export control exclusions is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology transfer agreements should contain export compliance provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Material transfer agreements and technology licenses should contain a general requirement that the parties will comply with U.S. export controls and embargoes to the extent applicable and that performance of the agreement is subject to such compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a license is required, the agreement should identify the license and ensure terms comply with license conditions. Termination provisions should provide rights if export/embargo compliance (e.g., required license) cannot be secured or maintained. Agreements should require the transferor to notify the transferee if materials/items/technology are export-controlled and require written consent of the proposed transferee prior to transfer to support identification of incoming controlled items/information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology transfer office role in institutional compliance program
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution should decide whether the technology transfer office will rely on faculty or a central export-control expert office to determine applicability of export controls and exclusions, or whether the technology transfer office will serve as a gatekeeper for transfers that may involve controlled materials/items or information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of the model, the technology transfer office should take specific steps to support export compliance (clauses in agreements, notification/consent procedures, termination rights, coordination with central compliance office). Consult institutional export-control experts when applicability is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: OFAC rules and scholarly publishing — permitted and proscribed activities
rubrics_metrics.description: OFAC historically found that peer review and editing of scholarly articles by entities subject to U.S. jurisdiction for authors from OFAC-sanctioned countries might constitute prohibited services, but guidance (Berman Amendment) and subsequent OFAC general licenses (Dec. 17, 2004) authorized certain activities related to paper or electronic publishing of manuscripts, books, journals and newspapers with nationals of Cuba, Sudan, and Iran.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OFAC licenses permit collaborating on creation/enhancement of written publications, augmenting publications with photographs/artwork/translation/explanatory text, substantive editing, and other transactions necessary and ordinarily incident to publishing and marketing written publications. Proscribed activities not covered include development/production/design/marketing of software and any activity controlled under EAR/ITAR. Academic/research institutions and personnel are not deemed part of the listed governments. The law remains unclear for other sanctioned countries; OFAC director guidance may permit limited peer review/copy editing for some countries but substantive co-authorship/editing with nationals of other sanctioned countries may require specific OFAC licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even if OFAC general license applies, assess EAR/ITAR controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Export controls under EAR or ITAR must still be assessed to determine whether information shared or created with a foreign national constitutes controlled technical data or technology and requires a license, even if the OFAC general license applies to the same information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete this assessment before sharing information with a foreign national (co-author, peer reviewer, editor) on a potentially export-controlled subject to avoid unintentional violations. OFAC licensing does not negate EAR/ITAR licensing requirements for controlled technologies, items, or services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public domain/public availability exclusions are broader than fundamental research exclusion but limited to prescribed methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The public domain/publicly available exclusions are broader in coverage than the fundamental research exclusion, but only the specific publication methods prescribed in the regulations qualify, regardless of how readily available information is globally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prescribed publication venues (public libraries, qualifying sales/subscriptions, patents/published patent applications, qualifying conferences and exhibitions, public websites) to rely on these exclusions. Remember these exclusions apply only to information/technical data, not to controlled physical items.
